Method

This chapter separates stages that are often collapsed into RLHF: source collection; task and rubric authoring; demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning; outcome ratings, preference pairs or ranked sets; reward or judge construction; policy optimization; executable environment design; evaluation; and documentation. The reviewed-work atlas below summarizes approved observations from exact inspected manifestations. A paper’s work identity counts once even when several versions exist. Bounded full_source review covers methods plus main results or worked examples and limitations; it does not claim all appendices, proofs, raw data or experiments were reproduced.

Analysis

Classical human-preference pipelines expose several independent design choices. The original trajectory-comparison study alternates interaction, human clip comparisons and reward fitting. The summarization study uses comparison-trained rewards and PPO with a KL penalty. InstructGPT ranks sets of responses and uses a separate unlabelled prompt pool for PPO. These are not merely different names for pairwise annotation: they differ in task construction, candidate sampling, comparison independence and the distribution exposed to optimization. A data purchase should preserve those distinctions in its manifest.

Evidence: cohort2.claim.humanprefs.async-method, cohort2.claim.humanprefs.clip-labels, cohort3.claim.summarize.pipeline, candidate.paperfull.instructgpt.human-ranking-sets, candidate.paperfull.instructgpt.unlabelled-ppo-inputs

Analysis

Preference optimization changes the training interface, rather than erasing data requirements. DPO fits a direct objective without a separate reward-model/RL loop; IPO studies a direct squared-loss formulation under a narrower experimental setting; ORPO combines chosen-response likelihood and odds-ratio loss without a frozen reference; KTO accepts desirable/undesirable labels. KTO experiments often transform existing pairs, so support for a binary interface is not evidence that all reported data were independently collected as binary judgments. Method comparison must retain label origin, model scale, candidate distribution and evaluation protocol.

Evidence: candidate.paperfull.dpo.direct-policy-objective, cohort2.claim.ipo.identity-objective, cohort2.claim.ipo.lm-scaling-limit, cohort2.claim.orpo.monolithic-loss, cohort2.claim.orpo.reference-free, cohort2.claim.kto.binary-signal, cohort2.claim.kto.paired-source-transformation

Analysis

Selection methods consume a candidate budget that is absent from a final retained-pair count. RAFT retains a high-reward fraction; statistical rejection sampling generates 64 candidates and subsamples eight in its standard experiment; SimPO’s instruct setting selects highest/lowest PairRM scores from five candidates; SPPO also uses five responses per prompt in its experiment. Their results cannot be explained by final training-row counts alone. A reproducible data and compute comparison should count generated candidates, judge calls, retained examples, rejected items, training updates and evaluation calls separately.

Evidence: cohort5.claim.raft.batch-selection, cohort5.claim.rso.budget, cohort5.claim.simpo.instruct-data, cohort5.claim.sppo.selection

Analysis

Process supervision targets intermediate steps, but step granularity and validation still differ. Let’s Verify Step by Step evaluates selection from a fixed generator and flags a large-scale comparison confound; Step-DPO contrasts next steps conditioned on earlier correct steps and warns that correct final answers can conceal bad intermediate reasoning; PRIME learns an online implicit process reward from outcome supervision. A buyer should distinguish human step labels from model-localized errors and from token rewards derived indirectly from final outcomes. None of these method labels alone proves faithful reasoning.

Evidence: cohort2.claim.process.fixed-generator-scope, cohort2.claim.process.large-comparison-confound, cohort5.claim.stepdpo.step-objective, cohort5.claim.stepdpo.step-limit, cohort8.claim.prime.online-prm, cohort8.claim.prime.token-reward

Analysis

Optimization papers also change normalization, sampling and infrastructure assumptions. DAPO filters all-correct or all-incorrect sampled groups and changes clipping and token aggregation; Dr. GRPO analyzes response-length and reward-standard-deviation biases; GSPO clips sequence ratios; VAPO adds value pretraining and length-adaptive advantages. These are specific recipes under their inspected experiments, not evidence of a universally best algorithm or a provider’s operational advantage. A buyer of training services should ask which recipe, reward definition, sampling budget and failure controls are actually implemented.

Evidence: cohort8.claim.dapo.dynamic-sampling, cohort8.claim.dapo.clip-higher, cohort8.claim.dapo.token-loss, cohort8.claim.drgrpo.length-bias, cohort8.claim.drgrpo.difficulty-bias, cohort8.claim.gspo.sequence-ratio, cohort8.claim.vapo.value-pretraining, cohort8.claim.vapo.length-adaptive

Analysis

Test-time adaptation needs a different evaluation contract. TTRL uses agreement with a sampled consensus as reward without target ground-truth labels; ReliableTTRL distinguishes population-majority error from finite-rollout variation; SelectTTRL fixes a selection rule without target answers but uses a separately labeled calibration set. Reporting only a final score hides adaptation data access and evaluation-budget differences. A fair comparison should state which test questions drive updates, which labels enter calibration, the total rollout budget, checkpoint-selection rule and whether every target question remains in the denominator.

Evidence: cohort8.claim.ttrl.consensus-reward, cohort8.claim.ttrl.test-adaptation, cohort8.claim.reliablettrl.error-types, cohort8.claim.reliablettrl.final-checkpoint, cohort8.claim.selectttrl.calibration, cohort8.claim.selectttrl.all-evaluated

Analysis

Synthetic and hybrid pipelines require stage-level lineage. Constitutional AI mixes human helpfulness with model harmlessness labels; ToolBench combines expert seed examples with ChatGPT instruction and trajectory generation; RLAIF-V uses model claim checking while its evaluation references include human corrections; Llama 3 collects new annotations and synthetic data across rounds. The practical requirement is a manifest identifying generator, prompt, seed material, selection model, correction roles and independent evaluation. A statement that humans were involved somewhere cannot establish that a particular training target is human-authored.

Evidence: cohort2.claim.constitutional.hybrid-label-origin, cohort4.claim.toolbench.synthetic-pipeline, cohort3.claim.rlaifv.claim-feedback, cohort3.claim.rlaifv.evaluation-human-proprietary, cohort5.claim.llama3.rounds

Analysis

Executable evaluation spans different abstractions. HumanEval checks short Python functions; SWE-bench checks issue-resolution patches; WebArena combines semantic and state checks; OSWorld uses desktop state evaluators; τ-bench checks database outcomes under interaction policies. Agents can receive different observation modes, budgets and simulator affordances. A single leaderboard column cannot remove these differences. The comparison should first ask whether the measured task and environment resemble the buyer’s deployment, then assess whether the scoring protocol detects the failures the buyer cares about.

Evidence: cohort4.claim.humaneval.task-construction, candidate.paperfull.swebench.regression-test-scoring, cohort2.claim.webarena.hybrid-evaluation, cohort4.claim.osworld.executable-outcome-judge, cohort4.claim.taubench.interactive-environment

Analysis

Research and professional-work benchmarks add substantial human design and review labor. RE-Bench records expert runs with tools; ScienceAgentBench uses subject-matter validation and separate execution verification; PaperBench aggregates binary rubric leaves and prohibits use of original authors’ code; TheAgentCompany records task-creation effort but lacks a professional human comparison in that iteration. These benchmarks make particular research activities observable, but their human baselines, time budgets and allowed resources differ. They cannot establish a general percentage of jobs that an agent can perform.

Evidence: cohort6.claim.rebench.human-count, cohort6.claim.rebench.human-tools, cohort6.claim.scienceagentbench.human-validation, cohort6.claim.paperbench.rubric, cohort6.claim.paperbench.original-code-rule, cohort6.claim.agentcompany.curation-labor, repair.binding.v1.cohort6.claim.agentcompany.human-baseline-limit

Analysis

Reward hacking and contamination should be studied as separate mechanisms. A learned reward can be overoptimized while human preference worsens; a program can pass supplied assertions by hard-coding tested inputs; a reasoning monitor can lose recall under direct optimization pressure; a public benchmark can be detected in training only under particular access and watermark assumptions. These examples motivate separate checks for objective misspecification, verifier gaming, monitor adaptation and training/test exposure. They do not establish the incidence of those failures in any provider’s current production service.

Evidence: cohort3.claim.summarize.overoptimization, cohort4.claim.mbpp.test-overfit, cohort7.claim.monitor.optimization, cohort8.claim.stamp.access-timing, cohort8.claim.stamp.paired-design

Analysis

Feedback-format comparison — ordinal ratings, rankings and binary signals preserve different information. HelpSteer2’s attribute ratings can retain multiple dimensions; InstructGPT’s ranked sets relate several responses under one prompt; Llama 2 adds preference strength; KTO can use one desirable/undesirable output. Converting all of them to binary pairs can discard attribute structure or strength and create correlated observations. The buyer should decide which information is required by the intended objective before paying for annotation. The reviewed studies do not establish one universally most efficient format, and the matched disagreement study specifically cautions against assuming paired preferences are inherently less ambiguous.

Evidence: next.claim.helpsteer2.attributes, candidate.paperfull.instructgpt.human-ranking-sets, cohort5.claim.llama2.preference, cohort2.claim.kto.binary-signal, cohort3.claim.disagreement.agreement-not-superiority

Analysis

Feedback-format comparison — rationale text and process labels answer different questions. The natural-language-feedback study uses author-written feedback to select refinements by embedding similarity; Innodata describes explanatory reasons for response scores; Step-DPO localizes the next erroneous step; DeepSeek-R1-Zero uses final accuracy and format rewards without a neural process reward. A rationale can be useful context without being a validated causal explanation or a correct intermediate proof. Procurement should distinguish the requested text artifact, its validation target and whether downstream training actually consumes it. These examples do not show that longer reasoning or more explanation is always better.

Evidence: cohort5.claim.languagefeedback.human-feedback, cohort5.claim.languagefeedback.selection, candidate.cohort3.innodata.explanatory-feedback, cohort5.claim.stepdpo.step-objective, cohort5.claim.deepseekr1.zero-reward

Analysis

Distribution comparison — offline preferences and current-policy rollouts can differ even when the file schema is identical. SLiC-HF notes mismatch between off-policy human-feedback data and SFT decodes; WPO reweights preference losses using current-policy response weights; REBEL permits a fixed or current-policy response distribution but samples both responses from the current policy in its described experiments. These methods make the candidate-generation distribution a material part of the recipe. A licensed preference dataset should therefore identify generating models, sampling settings and collection period, and a training-service proposal should explain whether fresh responses or labels are required.

Evidence: cohort5.claim.slichf.distribution-limit, cohort5.claim.wpo.weights, cohort5.claim.rebel.distribution, cohort5.claim.rebel.online-experiment

Analysis

Objective comparison — a scalar reward is a modeling choice, not a property guaranteed by human judgment. SPPO explicitly uses a two-player constant-sum preference game rather than requiring one transitive scalar ordering; WPO’s conceptual labeling construction assumes no conflicting pairs for a prompt; the instruction-tuning disagreement experiment observes task-dependent ambiguity. The analytical lesson is to state the aggregation assumptions and preserve counterexamples before fitting a reward. This does not prove that scalar models are inappropriate in every task; it identifies a condition to test when disagreements are central to the buyer’s use case.

Evidence: cohort5.claim.sppo.game, cohort5.claim.wpo.assumption, cohort3.claim.disagreement.instance-disagreement

Analysis

Budget comparison — optimization improvements can be inseparable from sample selection and validation conditions. Llama 3 rejection sampling generates 10–30 outputs per human-annotation prompt; DeepSeekMath samples 64 outputs per question in its described run; TTRL uses 64 voting responses and a 32-response training subsample. These are different compute and information budgets. A comparison based on retained examples, final model size or optimizer name alone is incomplete. Report total generations, token caps, judge calls and human checking, then distinguish training expenditure from evaluation expenditure. No cross-paper cost-normalized winner is computed here.

Evidence: cohort5.claim.llama3.sampling, cohort5.claim.deepseekmath.sampling-budget, repair.binding.ten.v1.cohort8.claim.ttrl.vote-then-sample

Analysis

Systems comparison — orchestration describes how computation moves, not whether feedback is valid. OpenRLHF uses separate rollout/training roles with vLLM and DeepSpeed and limits the inspected paper’s support to language models. HybridFlow routes data between parallel layouts and generally executes colocated roles sequentially to avoid contention or memory failures. A platform’s architectural support is therefore separate from a proof of label provenance, a task’s reward soundness or the performance of a trained model. For a systems purchase, ask for reproducible resource and data-flow measurements under the actual recipe while auditing feedback quality through a different protocol.

Evidence: cohort8.claim.openrlhf.vllm-deepspeed, cohort8.claim.openrlhf.language-scope, cohort8.claim.hybridflow.transfer-protocols, cohort8.claim.hybridflow.general-sequential

Analysis

Curation comparison — dataset selection can change task composition as well as nominal quality. AlpaGasus retains a model-scored subset of Alpaca and flags disproportionate removal of keyword-defined coding examples; DCLM’s classifier retains a top-scoring fraction under a defined positive/negative training set; DataComp permits filtered size to vary under fixed samples-seen compute. The defensible interpretation is that filters select a distribution according to their targets. A buyer should inspect what was removed and the resulting task mix, rather than infer that every discarded example was objectively bad or that a smaller selected set is universally better.

Evidence: cohort3.claim.alpagasus.selection, cohort3.claim.alpagasus.skill-balance, cohort3.claim.dclm.quality-filter, cohort3.claim.datacomp.controlled-design

Analysis

Evaluation comparison — win rate depends on who judges, what counts as a win and how ties are handled. The natural-language-feedback experiment counts ties as half a win; LIMA reports separate wins, ties and losses against dated responses; Llama 3 excludes slightly-better ratings from wins; RSO uses a three-rater majority. These figures cannot be pooled into a common preference advantage without the underlying protocol. A pilot should freeze the response population, judge rubric, blinding, tie rule and aggregation before comparing candidates, and report enough raw counts to reconstruct the stated metric.

Evidence: cohort5.claim.languagefeedback.test-protocol, cohort3.claim.lima.dated-human-comparison, cohort5.claim.llama3.human-win, cohort5.claim.rso.human-protocol

Analysis

Human-baseline comparison — the reference population and tools define the comparison. MMLU’s approximate expert level is an estimate rather than a measured panel across all subjects; RE-Bench allows human internet and LLM use; VisualWebArena avoids assigning task creators to their own tasks; WebShop gives humans HTML observations while models use simplified text. These are substantive design choices. A claim that an agent exceeds humans should identify which humans, prior task exposure, allowed tools, time limits and observation mode. The reviewed record does not support a general human-versus-AI capability ranking.

Evidence: candidate.paperfull.mmlu.estimated-expert-baseline, cohort6.claim.rebench.human-tools, cohort4.claim.visualwebarena.human-separation, cohort4.claim.webshop.observation-comparability

Analysis

Contamination comparison — tests detect particular kinds of overlap. MBPP’s normalized line-overlap analysis concerns eligible reference-program lines; BIG-bench’s canary is an intended training-exclusion signal; DeepSeekMath removes benchmark n-grams under its stated matching rules; STAMP requires pre-release watermarking and token-probability access. None of these procedures proves all forms of semantic or strategy-level independence. Buyers using public tasks should record exposure assumptions and run private or freshly authored holdouts where appropriate, while acknowledging that private construction also needs verification and rights review.

Evidence: cohort4.claim.mbpp.overlap-check, cohort4.claim.bigbench.contamination-canary, cohort5.claim.deepseekmath.decontamination, cohort8.claim.stamp.access-timing, cohort8.claim.stamp.one-sided-test

Analysis

Generalization comparison — different kinds of difficulty should remain separate. GPQA explicitly disclaims representativeness of scientific practice; HLE states that a high score alone would not demonstrate autonomous research; ScienceAgentBench selects Python partly because of annotator familiarity; RE-Bench warns that short clear tasks with supplied resources are unlike open-ended research. A buyer should use these benchmarks to locate specific weaknesses and design target-workflow tests. They do not justify extrapolating an exam score or a short-horizon optimization result into complete professional capability, employment substitution or general intelligence.

Evidence: cohort6.claim.gpqa.representativeness-limit, cohort6.claim.hle.capability-limit, cohort6.claim.scienceagentbench.python-selection, cohort6.claim.rebench.representativeness

Analysis

The additional annotation literature changes how the earlier technical methods should be read. Snow’s simplified temporal task and Gilardi’s agreed-human subset show that the reference population can change a model-versus-human comparison. HelpSteer2’s filtering changes the retained label population, while the label-error study shows that even corrected benchmark labels remain uncertain. A method comparison therefore needs three explicit objects: the items admitted, the rule defining reference truth and the items excluded before the headline result. This report treats those as experimental scope, rather than evidence of a universal labor or model advantage.

Evidence: cohort9.claim.snow.restricted-task, cohort9.claim.snow.temporal-vote, cohort9.claim.gilardi.gold-denominator, cohort9.claim.helpsteer2.agreement-selection, cohort9.claim.labelerrors.correction-limit

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: Consent in Crisis: The Rapid Decline of the AI Data Commons. The audited corpus sources are C4, RefinedWeb and Dolma. The head sample unions the top 2,000 domains by token count from each corpus into 3,950 domains. The random sample draws 10,000 domains from the 10,136,147-domain intersection and uses a random 2,000-domain subset for human annotation. The study reports inconsistencies between robots.txt signals and Terms of Service statements. Reading boundary: The study describes their differing crawl windows and filtering; paper version 2407.14933v1 is historical, not a current web-policy census.

Evidence: cohort7.claim.consentcrisis.corpora, repair.binding.ten.v1.cohort7.claim.consentcrisis.head, cohort7.claim.consentcrisis.random, cohort7.claim.consentcrisis.signals

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: CrowdWorkSheets: Accounting for Individual and Collective Identities Underlying Crowdsourced Dataset Annotation. The toxicity-labeling case study is explicitly hypothetical and presents its documentation responses as non-prescriptive and non-comprehensive. The framework recommends a dataset maintenance plan and consideration of when annotations can become outdated as language or standards change. CrowdWorkSheets organize documentation questions around stages of dataset construction, from task formulation to dissemination. The framework asks developers to connect annotator-pool selection to intended dataset uses and potentially impacted communities. Reading boundary: Its pay, risk disclosures and platform capabilities are illustrative assumptions, not observed operational facts or supplier relationships.

Evidence: cohort8.claim.crowdworksheets.hypothetical-example, cohort8.claim.crowdworksheets.maintenance, cohort8.claim.crowdworksheets.pipeline-framework, cohort8.claim.crowdworksheets.selection-rationale

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: Data Cards: Purposeful and Transparent Dataset Documentation for Responsible AI. Data Cards document critical dataset information across its life cycle and allow tailored templates rather than one fixed schema for every dataset. The design principles organize cards into self-contained modular sections and support multiple granularities and content types. The authors develop a participatory workshop approach that engages cross-functional stakeholders when creating transparent dataset metadata schemas. In the reported cases, Google Docs card templates supported collaboration but field-level iteration caused fragmentation and limited automation of collection. Reading boundary: Framework design; flexibility does not establish that a particular card is complete or accurate.

Evidence: cohort8.claim.datacards.lifecycle, cohort8.claim.datacards.modular, cohort8.claim.datacards.participatory, cohort8.claim.datacards.template-limits

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: Data Statements for Natural Language Processing: Toward Mitigating System Bias and Enabling Better Science. The proposed Annotator Demographic field includes relevant training of annotators and guideline developers. The proposed Language Variety field combines a BCP-47 tag with a prose description. For datasets assembled from existing datasets, the schema proposes an appendix containing the source datasets’ data statements. The proposed short-form data statement is a 60–100 word summary pointing to the long form. Reading boundary: Demographic and educational attributes are proposed documentation items; privacy and availability constrain collection/disclosure.

Evidence: cohort7.claim.datastatements.annotators, cohort7.claim.datastatements.language-variety, cohort7.claim.datastatements.provenance, cohort7.claim.datastatements.short-form

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: Datasheets for Datasets. The authors propose documenting a dataset’s motivation, composition, collection process and recommended uses. The questions and workflow were refined over roughly two years with multiple rounds of feedback. The paper states that datasheets alone are not a complete mitigation for unwanted societal bias or potential dataset harms. The authors intend datasheet creation to involve reflective human documentation rather than an automated creation process. For infrequently changing datasets, the authors recommend accompanying updated dataset versions with updated datasheets. The proposed collection-process documentation asks dataset creators to identify collection participants and their compensation. Reading boundary: Subsequent paragraphs describe example datasheets, product teams, researcher/practitioner/policy comments and legal feedback; this is author-reported development, not a controlled effectiveness trial.

Evidence: claim.datasheets.documentation, candidate.paperfull.datasheets.development-process, candidate.paperfull.datasheets.documentation-mitigation-limit, candidate.paperfull.datasheets.nonautomated-reflection, candidate.paperfull.datasheets.updated-version-docs, candidate.paperfull.datasheets.worker-compensation-disclosure

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: Documenting Large Webtext Corpora: A Case Study on the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus. The contamination analysis uses exact matches normalized for capitalization and punctuation and treats multi-component benchmark inputs separately. The authors leave quantification or removal of likely personally identifiable and copyrighted text in C4 for future work. C4 is derived from the April2019 Common Crawl snapshot with English identification and content filters, including a blocklist. The audit recommends documenting web metadata, the text included in a corpus, and the text excluded by filtering. Reading boundary: Exact input overlap does not alone establish that a benchmark label was present or that a trained model memorized it.

Evidence: cohort8.claim.documentingc4.exact-matching, cohort8.claim.documentingc4.future-audit, cohort8.claim.documentingc4.snapshot-filter, cohort8.claim.documentingc4.three-views

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models. The evaluation generates three pools of 200,000 samples, each sample 256 tokens long. The study identifies 604 unique memorized examples among its 1,800 selected candidates, reported as a 33.5% aggregate true-positive rate. For each of 18 generation-strategy/metric configurations, the study selects 100 samples from the metric’s top 1,000. The paper distinguishes training-data extraction of verbatim examples from inversion that reconstructs representative examples. Reading boundary: GPT-2 XL (1.5B parameters); strategies are top-n empty-sequence sampling, temperature sampling and Internet-conditioned sampling. Additional model identity support: physical p3 lines1–9.

Evidence: cohort7.claim.extraction.generation-pools, cohort7.claim.extraction.selected-results, cohort7.claim.extraction.selection, cohort7.claim.extraction.verbatim

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: How do data owners say no? A case study of data consent mechanisms in web-scraped vision-language AI training datasets. Copyright-notice detection applies regular expressions to captions and PaddleOCR-extracted image text. The study operationalizes a data owner as the actor embedding the image on a webpage. Two coders annotate domain category, license type and scraping policy, resolving disagreements through annotation or codebook changes. The study audits CommonPool small and medium scales, restricting to English captions using fastText. Reading boundary: Signal-detection method; notices and their absence are not a legal authorization determination.

Evidence: cohort7.claim.dataowners.copyright-detection, cohort7.claim.dataowners.owner-definition, cohort7.claim.dataowners.policy-coding, cohort7.claim.dataowners.scope

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: Improving Task Instructions for Data Annotators: How Clear Rules and Higher Pay Increase Performance in Data Annotation in the AI Economy. The experiment uses a 2×3 between-subjects design crossing instruction type with presence of an incentive. Besides image-label accuracy, the study measures perceived instruction helpfulness and perceived task difficulty separately. The study recruits 307 participants who completed the experiment through Prolific Academic. The payment design compares £4.50 base pay with a condition offering an additional single £3 incentive. Reading boundary: Instructions: rules, incomplete rules, standards. Task: classify 100 building-entrance images as barrier-free or not for a wheelchair user.

Evidence: cohort7.claim.instructions.factorial, cohort7.claim.instructions.measures, cohort7.claim.instructions.participants, cohort7.claim.instructions.payments

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: Minority Reports: Balancing Cost and Quality in Ground Truth Data Annotation. The pruning rule retains assignments involving unseen workers or tasks; otherwise it prunes when estimated minority-report probability exceeds a fixed threshold. Simulation quality is measured by comparing post-pruning majority votes against the counterfactual unpruned majority, using yes/no accuracy and F1. The paper defines a minority report as an annotator response that differs from the final majority-vote consensus for an image-crop question. The discussion cautions that RLHF ranked preferences can have high variability without a clear majority or a single notion of ground truth. Reading boundary: Prediction uses previously observed assignments and is recalibrated over time; a pruning decision is not a general worker competence judgment.

Evidence: cohort8.claim.minority.cold-start-retain, cohort8.claim.minority.evaluation-reference, cohort8.claim.minority.minority-definition, cohort8.claim.minority.rlhf-boundary

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: Model Cards for Model Reporting. The proposed quantitative analysis reports results by individual factors and their intersections. The proposed Intended Use section records primary uses, primary users and out-of-scope uses. The proposed Metrics section includes performance measures, decision thresholds and variation approaches. Where detailed training-data disclosure is infeasible, the paper advocates basic group-distribution information. Reading boundary: Section 4.7 also recommends confidence intervals where possible and metric variation; no universal fairness guarantee follows.

Evidence: cohort7.claim.modelcards.disaggregation, cohort7.claim.modelcards.intended-use, cohort7.claim.modelcards.metrics, cohort7.claim.modelcards.training-data

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: Sources of Disagreement in Data for LLM Instruction Tuning. On the full human dataset, quadratic-weighted kappa is 0.48 for SINGLE ratings and 0.43 for PREFERENCE combined scores; the authors find no evidence in this setup that preference annotation is easier or less ambiguous. Across the two human task formulations, the study reports instance-level disagreement correlation R=0.2 and ambiguity-set overlap 0.25, despite using the same annotators and data points. The zero-shot annotation experiment uses four instruction-tuned models from 1B to 8B; the 1B model has no reported human-label correlation, while the other three have correlation in 0.2–0.25. The human experiment selects720 Anthropic context/two-response instances, evenly split between helpful and harmless, and recruits 33 graduate-course annotators to perform both individual 1–5 quality ratings and paired preference/magnitude tasks. Reading boundary: This is a result for the studied population, generic quality instructions and sample; it does not establish all disagreement as noise.

Evidence: cohort3.claim.disagreement.agreement-not-superiority, cohort3.claim.disagreement.instance-disagreement, cohort3.claim.disagreement.llm-scope, cohort3.claim.disagreement.matched-design

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: The Data Provenance Initiative: A Large Scale Audit of Dataset Licensing & Attribution in AI. The initial audit covers 44 instruction/alignment finetuning collections comprising 1,858 individual datasets selected by experts for widespread use; overlapping datasets are intentionally not deduplicated to preserve collection design choices. The license protocol searches for creator-attributable licenses explicitly applying to data, distinguishes them from code licenses, and records permitted-use, attribution and share-alike categories with the strictest feature across multiple licenses. The provenance audit combines linked public metadata, human legal-expert annotation and GPT-4-assisted annotation; its topic annotation uses GPT-4 on a sample of 100 examples for up to 10 topics. The authors explicitly characterize their collection as best-effort categorization of self-reported licenses for research/transparency, not legal advice or a determination that the listed licenses are enforceable.

Evidence: cohort3.claim.provenance.audit-scope, cohort3.claim.provenance.data-license-protocol, cohort3.claim.provenance.mixed-annotation-roles, cohort3.claim.provenance.scope-caveat

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: The Data-Production Dispositif. Both authors analyze the instruction documents through structural, detailed-fragment and synoptic discourse-analysis stages. The investigation combines 55 interviews, participant observation and analysis of 210 instruction documents collected during 2019–2021 fieldwork. The Venezuela worker recruitment starts with convenience sampling and expands through snowball sampling. Fieldwork covers three crowdsourcing platforms operating in Venezuela and a data-work BPO in Buenos Aires. Reading boundary: Iterative interpretive analysis is contrasted with interview/observation material; not a controlled experiment or automated annotation-quality measurement.

Evidence: cohort7.claim.dataproduction.analysis, cohort7.claim.dataproduction.fieldwork, cohort7.claim.dataproduction.sampling, cohort7.claim.dataproduction.sites

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Documentation, labor and evidence quality: The Dataset Nutrition Label: A Framework To Drive Higher Data Quality Standards. The paper warns that the validity of a ground-truth comparison module depends on its reference dataset and can be harmed by a flawed comparator. The label uses stand-alone modules that can be combined to fit dataset type, information availability and specialist expertise. When all sampled rollouts for a prompt share one answer, the method caches them; if a later majority conflicts with that answer, it discards the new pseudo-pairs and uses a cache loss. PC-Dr.DPO sets each prompt’s robust temperature from its observed majority fraction, with weaker majorities receiving sharper within-prompt weighting. The analysis separates population-majority bias, where the policy’s modal answer is wrong, from finite-rollout variation, where sampled majorities differ from that mode. RLAIF-V generates candidate responses with the same model/distribution, decomposes factual response content into atomic claims, queries an open-source multimodal labeler with yes/no questions and constructs preference pairs for iterative DPO training. The authors acknowledge training costs and remaining hallucination despite improvements, and leave further trustworthiness gains for future methods. For the 146-sample MHumanEval response-level hallucination measure in v1, Table 1 reports 50.7% for OmniLMM 12B, 29.5% after RLAIF-V, and 45.9% for the compared GPT-4V condition. The 7B setting uses LLaVA 1.5 as instruction model and LLaVA-NeXT as labeler; the 12B setting uses OmniLMM as both instruction model and labeler, with four 4k-instruction iterations described for each. Reading boundary: Open-source training feedback does not mean the complete benchmark/evaluation workflow excludes humans or proprietary models. Table 4 defines99 dev and 261 test instructions; the prose’s images wording is inconsistent.

In this v1 summarization study, PaLM2 Large generates preference labels and PaLM2 Extra-Small initializes the models; RL uses modified A2C rather than PPO. Reviewed-work atlas — Safety, feedback and verification: Deliberative Alignment: Reasoning Enables Safer Language Models. The StrongREJECT human review uses at least two reviewers per prompt/answer pair, with an expert third reviewer arbitrating disagreements. AppendixA reports mean human assistance grade 1.020 for o1 and 1.335 for GPT-4o on its StrongREJECT review. For SFT filtering, completions are judged repeatedly and assigned the minimum judge score before high-score retention. SFT trains on original prompts with specification text removed, while keeping the generated reasoning/output as targets. During RL, the safety judge sees the policies but not the model’s chain-of-thought; this particular RL reward is used for o1 and o3-mini. Training completions are generated by a specification-agnostic base reasoning model prompted with category-relevant safety specifications. Reviewed-work atlas — Safety, feedback and verification: Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms: Methods, Scaling Behaviors, and Lessons Learned. The authors state that they do not know whether crowdworkers have expertise needed to assess some technical harms and that attack coverage is incomplete; the review workflow includes warnings, opt-out previews, support communication and a voluntary well-being survey. Self-reported attack success shows no clear model-size trend, while minimum harmlessness-model scores show RLHF models becoming harder to red-team with scale; harmful outputs still occur. At each dialogue turn, participants see two model responses and select the more harmful; after the conversation they rate attack success on a 0–4 scale, separately from the learned preference-model harmlessness score. A follow-up sample of 500 attacks each on 52B prompted and RLHF models receives three reviewer ratings per transcript; agreement including the attack author is Fleiss kappa0.32 on Likert ratings and 0.49 after binarization. The study’s red team comprises 324 US-based crowdworkers: 307 recruited through MTurk and 17 through Upwork; about 80% of attacks come from roughly 50 workers. Reading boundary: Worker-support descriptions do not establish absence of harm, and reduced average harmfulness does not establish a perfectly safe model.

The paper introduces Dolma as approximately 3T tokens across 5B documents from seven public data sources, alongside an open-source curation toolkit; its design primarily targets English text. Dolma’s general deduplication is within each source subset rather than across sources; its web pipeline uses URL, exact-document and exact-paragraph Bloom-filter stages, while code starts from The Stack’s prior near-deduplicated version. Reading boundary: This is a model-performance observation, not a privacy guarantee or a full PII-recall measurement. Buyers should test whether a proposed weighting rule preserves intended minority interpretations and improves independently checked outcomes before using it to exclude contributors or certify labels.

Analysis

Study assessment and change conditions — Quantifying and Avoiding Unfair Qualification Labour in Crowdsourcing. Qualification thresholds should be calibrated to the task rather than inherited as a universal proxy for competence. A paid pilot can compare a low-threshold route plus task-specific training with a stricter route, measuring output quality, exclusions and uncompensated preparation separately. These reports should not be counted as independent replications of one causal mechanism. Reviewed-work atlas — Repository engineering and executable verifiers: DeepSWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Original, Long-Horizon Engineering Tasks. DeepSWE contains 113 tasks across 91 active public repositories in TypeScript, Go, Python, JavaScript and Rust; its repository-selection rules require at least 500 GitHub stars and a permissive open-source license. For eight models with publicly reported SWE-Bench Pro results, the DeepSWE paper reports a 69.8-percentage-point pass-rate range on DeepSWE versus 29.7 points on SWE-Bench Pro. DeepSWE evaluates 16 model-and-reasoning-effort configurations under mini-swe-agent with a shared prompt and single bash tool, pinned to commit adfe20233d456104c38c3129161b54f0fd39f2c7. DeepSWE uses binary functional rewards without partial credit and does not score code readability, idiomatic style, maintainability, performance or documentation. Every DeepSWE task includes a prompt, executable functional verifier and reference solution; verifiers exercise public APIs and observable outputs rather than requiring the reference implementation's internal structure. DeepSWE accepts tasks only after LLM-assisted analysis and independent human review of the prompt, verifier, reference solution and diagnostic agent runs.

The headline interval measures rerun noise on the same 113 tasks, not task-selection uncertainty. Reviewed-work atlas — Scientific workflows and recoverable targets: GeneBench-Pro: Evaluating Multistage Statistical Reasoning in Genomics, Quantitative Biology, and Translational Biomedicine. The paper states that AI systems assisted problem design and review and manuscript editing, while the authors reviewed and approved the benchmark design, problem specifications, validation targets, evaluation results and final manuscript. The reported evaluation attempted ten independent runs per model-problem pair for standard evaluations and five for GPT Pro (Extended) and Claude Opus; container, tooling, provider and response-format errors were excluded from per-problem pass-rate estimates. The paper attributes benchmark conception, problem implementation and review, external-review coordination and benchmark testing to Jeremy Li, and model evaluation runs to Andrew Ho; both authors drafted and revised the manuscript. The reported primary metric uses Python binary grading: every prespecified target field must satisfy its exact-match rule or absolute numeric tolerance for the run to pass, and the free-text reasoning field is collected for qualitative analysis but is not graded. The paper reports evaluation of the full 129-problem suite across 60 model configurations, including mainline GPT, GPT Pro and non-GPT baseline rows.

Study construction and protocol — GeneBench-Pro: Evaluating Multistage Statistical Reasoning in Genomics, Quantitative Biology, and Translational Biomedicine. The paper defines overall pass rate as the unweighted mean of per-problem pass rates across 129 problems and reports 95% hierarchical bootstrap intervals from 20,000 resamples, resampling problems and repeated runs within problems. The authors’ manual review of selected GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Sol reasoning traces suggests a notice-act gap: failures may identify local diagnostics without sufficiently revising downstream statistical methods or QC. The reported harness used a Linux Docker environment with Python and R scientific and bioinformatics software and no internet access, restricting agents to the prompt, staged files, installed software and model-internal knowledge. The inspected preprint banner states that the preprint was not certified by peer review and is available under CC-BY-NC 4.0. The paper’s construction description and example prompt tell agents that analytical reasoning quality is graded alongside numerical correctness, while its Methods section states that free-text reasoning is not graded. The paper reports no additional uniform wall-clock budget imposed by the evaluation harness, while runs remained subject to provider and platform behavior in the evaluation stack.

Study assessment and change conditions — GeneBench-Pro: Evaluating Multistage Statistical Reasoning in Genomics, Quantitative Biology, and Translational Biomedicine. Recoverable target design is central: the correct estimand is what staged observations support, rather than an inaccessible simulation parameter. Binary all-field scoring nevertheless collapses an early failure and a late statistical mistake. Confidence is high in those measurement distinctions and moderate in the curated scientific-workflow relevance. The notice-act explanation is selected-trace interpretation, not a measured chain-length law. Independent review of unreviewed tasks, resolved prompt/grader wording and representative real-data studies would change confidence in generalization.

Reviewed-work atlas — Health conversations and rubric measurement: HealthBench: Evaluating Large Language Models Towards Improved Human Health. The v1 main text reports that 262 physicians created HealthBench tasks over eleven months, with practice experience in 60 countries and 26 specialties, and that all physician cohort members were compensated. The v1 paper describes most conversations as model-synthetic from physician-designed situation types, with additional physician red-team conversations and transformed HealthSearchQA queries described as released by Google; o1-preview filters for relevance, realism, self-consistency and complete messages. The v1 paper validates model grading against physician grades on the 34 predefined consensus criteria and selects GPT-4.1 as its default grader; it acknowledges that most example-specific criteria were written by individual physicians and were not validated by other physicians. The v1 paper grades each criterion as met or not met, applies its signed nonzero point weight from minus ten to ten, divides the sum by the available positive points per example, and clips the mean example score to zero through one.

Reviewed-work atlas — Human-time calibration and composite evaluation: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks. The paper reports approximately eight attempts per agent/task pair and uses general agent scaffolds without task-specific prompting, except that SWAA uses a simple prompting scaffold. The authors state that task-completion horizons depend on the task distribution and on the human reference population’s skill and context. For HCAST, task durations are calculated using the geometric mean time of successful human baseline attempts, with manual estimates for tasks lacking successful baselines; RE-Bench instead receives a fixed eight-hour duration rating. A separate internal-repository study uses five original issues and has maintainers grade submitted solutions manually, rather than requiring every issue to have an automatic checker. The authors label HCAST and RE-Bench tasks for the presence of 16 defined messiness factors and sum those labels into a score from zero to 16. The paper says supplementary material will provide code and data for some core figures, while the full codebase is infeasible to publicize and anonymize; code for additional figures may be provided on reviewer request.

Study construction and protocol — Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks. The analysis binarizes task scores using task-specific human-performance thresholds: HCAST uses its target score and RE-Bench uses the average score of human runs lasting seven to nine hours. Section 2.1 describes a composite evaluation suite containing 97 selected HCAST tasks, seven RE-Bench environments and 66 Software Atomic Actions tasks. The method fits an agent-specific logistic model against log human task duration; the fitted horizon is the duration with predicted 50% success, and each task receives weight equal to the inverse square root of its task-group size.

Study result — Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks. The paper extrapolates historical trends toward a one-month horizon defined as approximately 167 human working hours, while treating that result as conditional on continued trends and transfer to real-world software work. The reported 80%-success horizons are four to six times shorter than the 50%-success horizons, while the fitted doubling times are similar at 204 and 207 days respectively. For the reported 2019–2025 model series, the paper estimates a 207-day doubling time with a 95% bootstrapped interval of 166–240 days, using 10,000 resamples over task groups, tasks and runs.

Reviewed-work atlas — Medical question construction and validation: MedXpertQA: Benchmarking Expert-Level Medical Reasoning and Understanding. The v1 paper assesses leakage risk before and after rewriting with GPT-4o outputs, using perplexity and similarity to collected explanations measured by ROUGE-L and edit distance. The v1 methods describe model rephrasing intended to preserve question information, removal of weak distractors and setting the final choice counts to ten for Text and five for MM, using GPT-4o-2024-11-20 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet-20241022. The v1 paper describes filtering an initial 37,543-question medical exam/textbook bank using model votes, difficulty thresholds based on human-response Brier scores and prior expert difficulty ratings, and semantic-similarity filtering.

Reviewed-work atlas — Professional tasks, judging and economic interpretation: The AI Productivity Index (APEX). APEX-v1.0 grades each rubric criterion with three judges: o3 with thinking Low, Gemini 2.5 Pro with thinking Off, and Sonnet 4 with thinking Off. It uses a two-of-three or unanimous majority for each binary criterion grade. The APEX-v1.0 paper compares its model scores with publicly reported HLE, MMLU Pro, MMMU Val and GPQA scores and reports a mean cross-benchmark correlation of 0.79. The captured APEX-v1.0 paper parses evidence PDFs and CSVs with Reducto and appends the parsed material to each task prompt, using one parsing strategy across models and avoiding the closed models' native file-handling APIs. The APEX-v1.0 paper explicitly cautions that rubric scores need not track real-world value linearly: a response scoring 60% might be effectively useless when value is stage-gated. The APEX-v1.0 judge panel agrees with expert Pass/Fail labels on 89% of 5,818 criterion ratings collected for responses from one model, Gemini 2.5 Pro with thinking On.

Study construction and protocol — The AI Productivity Index (APEX). In APEX-v1.0, repeating each judge three times on responses from one arbitrarily selected model, Grok 4, yields reported internal agreement of 99.5% for o3 Low, 99.4% for Gemini 2.5 Pro Off and 99.6% for Sonnet 4 Off. APEX-v1.0 rubrics lack negative criteria that penalize incorrect or irrelevant statements, so passing many positive criteria does not guarantee that a response contains fewer errors. The APEX-v1.0 observational comparison reports mean scores of 55.8% for models offering thinking tokens versus 40.4% for the others, with 16 of 23 models in the thinking group. APEX-v1.0 collects three responses from every model for each prompt and uses the median of their three scored responses for the leaderboard and analysis.

Study result — The AI Productivity Index (APEX). In the captured APEX-v1.0 experiment, GPT 5 with thinking High has the highest reported mean score, 64.2%, followed by Grok 4 at 61.3% and Gemini 2.5 Flash with thinking On at 60.4%.

Study limitations — The AI Productivity Index (APEX). The original 200-case August 2025 experiment uses median-of-three responses and a three-judge criterion majority. Its 89% expert agreement covers 5,818 ratings from one response model, with expert labels not themselves reviewer-validated. Near-99.5% judge repeatability covers another selected model and is not correctness. Cross-benchmark correlations have missing model scores. Thinking-group comparisons confound recency and model type, without a causal ablation.

Study assessment and change conditions — The AI Productivity Index (APEX). Providing the needed evidence in context makes this a professional response test rather than a live information-retrieval workflow. Positive rubric completion can coexist with unsupported extra claims because negative criteria are absent. Confidence is high in those restrictions and unestablished for economic value. A buyer should test decisive negative conditions and compare the full response distribution before choosing a best-of or median protocol. Representative prospective work, independent judge calibration and matched thinking on/off experiments would change the operational interpretation.

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Annotation methodology and maintenance: Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation. The authors propose keyboard-bound choices and simple annotation tasks, varying option order to reduce priming and showing all alternatives on one screen to avoid scrolling bias. The paper distinguishes intra-annotator stability over time from inter-annotator reproducibility and discusses simple agreement, Kappa variants and Krippendorff alpha as evaluation measures. The authors recommend developing the codebook with annotators and monitoring agreement so that category definitions remain stable as the scheme evolves. For contrastive annotation, the paper describes a common core scheme with language-specific extensions and illustrates this approach with English and Spanish thematic-field annotation in CONTRANOT. The paper discusses reconciliation and adjudication of annotation disagreements, cautioning that reconciliation can raise agreement scores while risking overtraining or drift and recommending it mainly for initial training. The paper emphasizes ownership and distribution licensing when maintaining annotated corpora and describes distributing annotation layers separately when the underlying corpus cannot be distributed directly.

Source-backed finding

Study construction and protocol — Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation. The 2010 paper describes the QDAP annotation center at the University of Pittsburgh as performing annotation for hire for NLP and Political Science clients. The paper proposes an iterative annotation pipeline that selects representative text, instantiates a theory in a codebook, pilots annotation and agreement checks, scales annotation with intermediate checks, and trains and evaluates automation on held-out annotated material. The paper distinguishes corpus representativeness from category balance and describes a tradeoff between preserving natural category frequencies and obtaining enough rare-category examples for learning or theoretical analysis.

Study result scope — Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation. This entry synthesizes the 2010 paper’s methodological proposals and cautions. Its illustrative agreement gate is not an experimental validation of a universal threshold, and no new controlled performance result is manufactured for this atlas.

Study limitations — Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation. This 2010 methodological paper proposes procedures and illustrates tradeoffs; it does not supply a current controlled estimate of the best interface or agreement threshold. Its Figure 1 90% gate is illustrative, and later discussion says acceptable agreement depends on use and can be lower for complex tasks. Historical QDAP annotation-for-hire is not evidence of a current qualifying supplier.

Analysis

Study assessment and change conditions — Towards a Science of Corpus Annotation. The strongest connection to modern feedback work is that codebooks, interfaces, training and downstream use jointly define label quality. Agreement can rise through undocumented shared instructions or reconciliation without making the labels more reproducible. Confidence is high in using the paper to pose diligence questions and unmeasured for a universal numeric rule. A pilot should archive each guideline change and compare stability on fresh annotators. Controlled interface studies and downstream validation would change which recommendations merit mandatory acceptance criteria.

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Aggregation, transcription and competition measurement: VLDB 2021 Crowd Science Challenge on Aggregating Crowdsourced Audio Transcriptions. ROVER aligns submitted word sequences and votes at each token, allowing an output different from every worker submission; RASA and HRRASA instead choose one submitted transcription. The shared-task dataset was constructed from normalized English Wikipedia and BookCorpus sentences, synthesized as audio with Yandex SpeechKit and transcribed on Toloka by at least five different workers per recording. Table 1 lists 9,700 training recordings with 67,900 transcriptions and 4,502 test recordings with 31,514 transcriptions; the test set is split into 1,500 public and 3,002 private recordings. The competition scores mean per-recording word accuracy, AWAcc = mean(max(0, 1−WER(r))) × 100%, using JiWER for each recording; live competition scores use the public test subset and final standings use the private subset. The authors report releasing the raw texts, baseline methods and scoring program, and link the Toloka/VLDB2021_Crowd_Science_Challenge repository. The report identifies Toloka as the platform used to collect the shared-task transcriptions and thanks the Toloka team for providing the crowdsourcing budget.

Source-backed finding

Study result — VLDB 2021 Crowd Science Challenge on Aggregating Crowdsourced Audio Transcriptions. The winning system fine-tuned a BART summarization model on the shared-task data, shuffled input transcriptions for augmentation and normalized British word forms to American forms; it achieved reported private-test AWAcc of 95.73%.

Evidence: candidate.next8.vldb2021.paper.winning-method.v3

Source-backed finding

Study limitations — VLDB 2021 Crowd Science Challenge on Aggregating Crowdsourced Audio Transcriptions. Table 1 separates 9,700 training and 4,502 test recordings; section 2 instead describes 99,414 transcriptions for 9,700 recordings. The mismatch is retained, not repaired by inventing a denominator. Audio is synthesized from normalized texts, so this is not natural recorded conversational speech. AWAcc averages clipped per-recording accuracy rather than computing one corpus WER. Public and private standings use different test subsets.

Analysis

Study assessment and change conditions — VLDB 2021 Crowd Science Challenge on Aggregating Crowdsourced Audio Transcriptions. Choosing an existing transcription and constructing a token-voted transcription are different deliverables. The latter can recover useful fragments while creating an output no worker submitted. Confidence is high in that distinction and moderate in applying the shared-task lesson to similarly synthesized audio. A buyer should compare per-recording errors, rare words and cross-worker dependence, preserving the raw submissions. Natural-speech replications and independently checked reference normalization would change confidence in transfer.

Source-backed finding

Reviewed-work atlas — Visual grounding and crowd collection: WSDM Cup 2023 Challenge on Visual Question Answering. The dataset contains 45,199 question-image instances: 38,990 training, 1,705 public-test and 4,504 private-test instances. The evaluation averages intersection over union between each predicted answer box and its ground-truth box; each item IoU is the boxes intersection area divided by their union area. Toloka workers selected images containing objects they found interesting, composed questions about those objects and then marked the answering objects with bounding boxes to exclude unanswerable questions. The CodaLab competition froze its dataset before the challenge, used public-test prediction submissions during evaluation and then required container-image solutions for organizer execution on the private test set to determine winners. The authors report releasing the complete dataset and ground truth after the competition under the same CC BY license as the selected COCO image subset, with Zenodo, Hugging Face, Kaggle and GitHub release links. The Toloka Visual Question Answering Challenge takes an image and an English question and asks for a bounding box around the object answering that question.

Source-backed finding

Study result — WSDM Cup 2023 Challenge on Visual Question Answering. A separate Toloka annotation round measured non-expert human performance without providing ground truth; the report gives mean IoU of 0.87 ± 0.01 across the three dataset subsets. The winning system used a Uni-Perceiver backbone, ViT-Adapter localization and DINO prediction head with an auxiliary loss and test-time augmentation; Table 3 reports its private-test reproduction score as 76.347 on the displayed IoU ×100 scale. The starter baseline uses YOLOR to propose candidate rectangles, applies CLIP to compare the question with each bounded image region and selects the highest-similarity candidate.

Study limitations — WSDM Cup 2023 Challenge on Visual Question Answering. Question/image instances are not unique images or workers. About 20% of boxes overlap COCO rectangles and all such instances enter training; pretrained-COCO access was allowed. The non-expert baseline is a separate annotation round, and alpha uses 1−IoU as response distance. The dataset DOI is distinct from this CEUR paper identity. Release licensing is an author statement, without an independent per-image rights audit.

Study assessment and change conditions — WSDM Cup 2023 Challenge on Visual Question Answering. The operational lesson is to specify spatial ground truth and its disagreement geometry. A box-overlap metric measures localization, not whether a free-form answer is useful, and the separate crowd round cannot be treated as task-author self-agreement. Confidence is high in these distinctions and moderate in the collection protocol as a design reference. A buyer should inspect ambiguous object boundaries, unanswerable questions and image reuse across splits. New-image heldouts with independent annotators and container replay would change external-validity confidence.

Analysis

Cross-study synthesis — output completion, statistical recovery and rubric quality are different targets. GeneBench-Pro requires every prespecified output field and does not grade its reasoning text; HealthBench aggregates signed criterion weights; APEX-v1 reports median criterion completion; ProgramBench requires all behavioral tests and no cheating flag. A shared percentage sign is not a shared unit. Confidence is high in these distinctions and unmeasured for a universal best metric. A buyer should choose the actual accepted deliverable, identify decisive failures and retain the diagnostic vector behind the aggregate. Matched evaluations with independently accepted outputs would change the relative usefulness of each score.

Inspected-code and documentation supplement — MMLU and SWE-bench. At MMLU creator commit 4450500f923c49f1fb1dd3d99108a0bd9717b660, evaluate.py requests five demonstrations by default, reduces their count under context cropping, selects the highest A–D token log probability and reports sample-weighted aggregate accuracy. This code inspection did not execute the benchmark or establish byte-level identity with the separately pinned HF release. SWE-bench collection documentation at commit 02e7a74ffd0b707aab73d203fe87bdc7c76afc8e describes PR/issue scraping, gold patch/test requirements, installation setup and execution-based validation; it does not independently prove that every original instance followed every step. Original proposal-stage notes remain historical; the current approved records and exact receipts control admission.

Evidence: next.claim.mmlu.evaluation, next.claim.swebench.collection

Analysis

Reasoning-data provenance has at least three separate accounting units: the original question, the generated solution trace and the verification decision. AM distinguishes reused material from its own DeepSeek-R1 responses; s1K-1.1 retains the same questions while changing traces; Light-R1 describes curriculum selection followed by generated correct/incorrect pairs. The implication is to preserve prompt-source, response-source and verification lineage separately. A new teacher response does not establish a new independent question, a human preference or a proved-correct solution. Confidence is high in these documented distinctions and unmeasured in their comparative training benefit. Item-level lineage and matched independent verification would change the uncertainty about actual coverage.

Analysis

A benchmark judge’s information boundary is part of the measured system. Chartography’s final-answer judge does not receive the chart; GDP.pdf’s criterion judge receives neither PDF nor reference answer; Harvey LAB scopes its calls to declared output files. Those observations support an audit question before interpreting scores: can the judge actually observe each fact needed for the criterion, and where is the required evidence encoded? They do not demonstrate that these judges are inaccurate. Confidence is high in treating context visibility as a protocol condition; judge error remains unmeasured here. A blinded expert study with missing-evidence, contradictory-evidence and valid alternative-output cases could validate or revise the proposed acceptance design.

Evidence: candidate.add17.chartography.grading.v2, candidate.add17.gdp-pdf.evaluation.v2, candidate.third11.harvey-lab.criteria.v3

Analysis

Strict task completion, partial-credit quality and repeated-attempt reliability answer different questions even within one release. ComplexConstraints separates all-criteria success from mean criterion satisfaction; Harvey LAB’s two-judge average permits a half score while its strict all_pass requires both judges; APEX-SWE separates pass@1 and pass@3 and keeps supplementary rubric scores outside its leaderboard. This supports reporting a small metric vector rather than converting every percentage to a common success rate. Confidence is high in the mathematical distinction and unknown in any cross-benchmark performance ordering. A common task population with a frozen rubric, judge context, repeat policy and failure denominator would be necessary for a narrower comparison.

Evidence: candidate.add17.complexconstraints.evaluation.v2, candidate.third11.harvey-lab.dual-scoring.v2, candidate.third11.apex-swe.quality-rubrics.v2, candidate.third11.apex-swe.verification.v2

Analysis

Environment packaging and completed validation are separate observations. Multi-SWE-bench documents test-transition filtering and a manual review stage; the initial Multi-SWE-RL construction omits that manual stage. Terminal-Bench documents oracle/dummy controls and exploit review while retaining residual flaws; PostTrain Arena explicitly distinguishes static source acceptance from planned dynamic checks that runs do not yet await. The analytical implication is to request evidence for each gate rather than inherit confidence from a Dockerfile or a shared construction pipeline. Confidence is high in the documented stage boundaries and unmeasured for actual task failure rates. Independent replay of the oracle, no-op controls, alternate valid solutions and exploit cases would change the buyer’s operational confidence.

Evidence: candidate.normal12.multi-swe-bench.dual-review.v3, candidate.normal12.multi-swe-bench.test-filter.v2, candidate.normal12.multi-swe-rl.verification-boundary.v2, candidate.normal12.terminal-bench.verification.v4, candidate.add17.posttrain.quality-gates.v2

Analysis

Difficulty selection changes what an absolute score represents. BrowseComp screens for difficult retrieval; AdvancedIF retains final-turn instruction failures against a supplied model; GDP.pdf requires meaningful failures by frontier models; µ-MATH intentionally selects text-only problems for judging difficulty rather than representing all U-MATH tasks. These observations support treating each as a stress distribution with an explicit selection rule. They do not yield the frequency of failure in an ordinary buyer workload or the share of a profession that can be automated. Confidence is high in that sampling limit. A prospectively sampled buyer workload, including routine and difficult cases, could establish an appropriately scoped external rate.
